drills.q: What does TCP guarantee that UDP doesn't, and is UDP's checksum mandatory?
drills.a: TCP guarantees ordered delivery, reliability (ACK+retransmit), flow control, congestion control, and connection state; UDP guarantees only a checksum and port demultiplexing. The checksum is optional in IPv4 (can be all-zero) but mandatory in IPv6 -- saying 'UDP has no checksum' is wrong.

drills.q: Why would you choose UDP over TCP for a real-time video call, with numbers?
drills.a: A jitter buffer tolerates ~20-60ms of jitter; a single TCP retransmit round trip on a 100ms RTT path already exceeds that, producing a multi-hundred-ms perceptible stall. UDP just drops the late frame and the codec conceals it -- worse for one frame, imperceptible over the call; TCP's 'fix' is the actually worse outcome here.

drills.q: Walk through TCP's three-way handshake and its cost.
drills.a: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK, establishing sequence number state in both directions. Costs 1 RTT before any application data flows, unless TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413) lets a returning client ride data on the initial SYN via a cookie from a prior connection.

drills.q: Explain head-of-line blocking's scope in TCP, HTTP/2-over-TCP, and QUIC.
drills.a: TCP: connection-scoped -- one lost segment blocks all later bytes on that connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, so it inherits that same connection-scoped stall across every stream. QUIC gives each stream independent loss recovery, shrinking the blast radius to the stream -- but a stream is still internally ordered, so it's still HOL-blocked within itself.

drills.q: Why does QUIC run over UDP instead of defining a new IP-layer protocol?
drills.a: Ossification: a new transport protocol number would be dropped or mishandled by most middleboxes/NATs/firewalls, and kernel-level support requires an OS upgrade on every endpoint. UDP is already universally passable, so QUIC implements reliability, congestion control, and encryption in userspace libraries that can iterate at application-release speed instead of kernel-release speed.

drills.q: What is QUIC connection migration and why can't TCP do it?
drills.a: A QUIC connection is identified by a Connection ID chosen at handshake time, not the 4-tuple (src/dst IP+port), so it survives a client's IP changing (Wi-Fi to cellular) without a new handshake. TCP has no equivalent because a TCP connection IS the 4-tuple; changing any element makes the kernel see a different connection entirely.

drills.q: Design the transport choice for a multiplayer game sending 20 position updates/sec per player, and explain what changes for a kill-confirmation event.
drills.a: Position updates: UDP, unreliable and unordered, since a late retransmitted update is already stale and superseded by the next tick anyway -- add a thin payload sequence number so clients discard out-of-order arrivals without transport-level retransmission. Kill confirmations and inventory/chat: need reliability, so use a lightweight reliable layer over UDP (ENet-style ACK+retry, or QUIC's reliable streams) rather than opening a second TCP connection, which would add its own handshake cost and a second congestion-control domain.

drills.q: Why does DNS use UDP, and when does it fall back to TCP?
drills.a: A query and response fit in one packet in the common case (<=512 bytes without EDNS0, up to 4096 with it), so UDP avoids a handshake -- 1 RTT total. Falls back to TCP when the response would be truncated (TC bit set): large record sets, DNSSEC-signed responses, or zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR, TCP-only by spec).

drills.q: A dropped packet on a TCP connection carrying an HTTP/2 multiplexed API gateway causes p99 latency spikes but flat p50. Diagnose, and describe how you'd confirm it.
drills.a: TCP enforces in-order delivery to the application, so one lost segment blocks every later byte on that connection -- including unrelated HTTP/2 streams sharing it -- producing an intermittent stall visible in p99 without moving the median (most connections at any instant aren't experiencing loss). Confirm by correlating p99 spikes with retransmission counters (netstat -s, ss -ti showing 'retrans') on the affected hosts; 1:1 correlation confirms HOL blocking rather than app-side slowness.

drills.q: Your team wants to move internal gRPC traffic from HTTP/2 to QUIC/HTTP-3. What do you ask first, and why might 'HTTP/3 is faster' not apply here?
drills.a: First: do we have workloads with genuinely concurrent independent streams per connection suffering TCP HOL blocking today -- if most RPC connections carry one dominant call at a time, there's little to gain. Second: can we decrypt/inspect QUIC traffic in existing observability tooling. Third: what's the CPU headroom, since loss recovery and crypto move to userspace. QUIC's latency win comes from combining transport+TLS handshake into 1 RTT and independent-stream recovery -- neither applies uniformly to already-warm, connection-pooled internal RPC the way it does to a browser's cold connection to a public CDN edge.

drills.q: What is a raw IP socket, who actually uses one, and would you use one in an application service?
drills.a: SOCK_RAW bypasses the kernel's TCP/UDP demultiplexing to construct/inspect IP packets directly, requiring elevated privileges. Used by ping/traceroute (ICMP construction), packet crafting/capture tools (scapy, hping3), and protocols running directly over IP with no port (OSPF, protocol 89). Essentially never in application services -- if you need custom transport semantics, build on UDP (normal privilege, portable) rather than raw IP.

drills.q: Explain TCP congestion control's role versus flow control, and what breaks without it.
drills.a: Flow control protects the receiver (bounded by its buffer, advertised via rwnd); congestion control protects the shared network path from being overwhelmed by all flows sharing it, inferred via loss or (with BBR) measured delay. Without congestion control, a sender blasts at line rate regardless of path conditions, causing cascading loss across every flow on a shared bottleneck -- the 1980s 'congestion collapse' problem Van Jacobson's algorithms were built to prevent. This is exactly why any UDP-based protocol used at scale, QUIC included, must implement its own congestion control in userspace.

drills.q: Does moving to QUIC eliminate the need for application-level timeouts and retries?
drills.a: No. QUIC fixes transport-level connection-establishment latency (1-RTT vs TCP+TLS's 2+ RTTs) and shrinks loss-recovery blast radius across independent streams, but says nothing about application-level failure -- a slow or wedged upstream still needs request timeouts, and a genuinely failed request still needs an idempotency-aware retry policy. Transport reliability and application resilience are orthogonal.

drills.q: Rank TCP, UDP, and QUIC by RTTs to first application byte for a cold connection, and state the one case where QUIC's stream-independence buys nothing.
drills.a: TCP+TLS 1.3: 2+ RTTs (1 TCP handshake + 1 TLS). Plain TCP (no TLS): 1 RTT. QUIC: 1 RTT in the common case, combining transport and TLS 1.3 handshake into one flight (0-RTT possible on resumption, with replay caveats). QUIC's HOL-blocking fix buys nothing when the workload is a single large sequential transfer over one stream -- the benefit is specific to multiple concurrent independent streams sharing a connection.
